summary: This unit teaches you to evaluate an existing or newly built electrical installation: agreeing the purpose and scope, gathering evidence from records, inspection, sampling, logging and thermal imaging, judging capacity, balance, power quality, condition and energy use, ranking risks, comparing options with costs, and reporting clearly to the client. You will also learn how to evaluate after a flood or hurricane and how to prove that improvements worked.

blocks.p: To **evaluate** an installation is to find out, with evidence, how good it is: is it safe, is it big enough, is it in good condition, does it meet the specification, and is it wasting energy? Then you tell the client what to do about it, in order of importance, with costs. Clients ask for evaluations before buying a building, before adding load, after damage, when faults keep happening, when bills are too high, and before accepting new work from a contractor.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Settle in writing what is evaluated, what questions are answered, access and shutdown times.
Collect drawings, test records, maintenance logs and a year of power bills; talk to the maintenance staff; allow for gaps in the records.
Choose a team, calibrated instruments, a risk assessment and permits.
Inspect boards, wiring and equipment; take a fair sample and widen it when faults appear.
Use a power logger and clamp meter to find peaks, line balance, voltage, power factor and harmonics.
Find hot connections safely, on load, and rank them.
Compare readings with the design and specification; spot trends in test results; calculate spare capacity.
Take a baseline, work out savings and simple payback, and check results afterwards.
Score risks, compare repair, upgrade and replacement, and give costed options.
Write a clear report, present it danger first, and measure again after changes.

ul: Before buying or leasing an old building, such as an old factory in Spanish Town.
A **change of use**: a house becoming a shop.
**Planned extra load**: new A/C units or a computer lab.
**Damage** after a fire, flood or hurricane.
Repeated trips, flickering lights or faults.
Acceptance of a contractor's new installation against the design, specification and contract.
High power bills or a charge for low power factor.

blocks.note: A change of business name is not a reason to evaluate an installation. A good evaluation always starts from a clear question: **what does the client need to decide?**
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Before work starts, agree **in writing**: the purpose; the areas and systems covered and not covered; the questions to be answered (condition, capacity, safety, energy); the access you will have; and when shutdowns are possible. Names of tenants' staff, rents and colour schemes are not part of the brief.

blocks.h: Criteria: what is it measured against?

head: Situation
Evaluate against
rows: A new installation offered for acceptance
The design, the specification and the contract; not the contractor's opinion, nor the building next door.
The code the Centre uses, the original design where there is one, the manufacturers' ratings, and the client's needs.
The rating of the service, main switch, main cable and board, and the logged demand.

ul: Drawings, single-line diagrams and board schedules.
Test records and certificates, and past inspection reports.
Maintenance logs and a list of faults.
A year of power bills (energy used, maximum demand, power factor, charges).
Plans for new loads.

blocks.p: If **no drawings or records can be found**, do not pass the installation because nothing shows that it has failed, and do not assume every cable is the size printed on its breaker. Note the gap in the report, trace and record the key circuits yourself, and allow more time.

blocks.h: Plan the team and the safety

flow: Agree the scope, access and shutdown times
Collect drawings, records, logs and bills
Choose the team and give each person a role
Check instruments are calibrated and in date
Write the risk assessment and obtain permits and authorisation
Brief the team and the client's staff

blocks.note: Before a board cover is removed for readings (for example with a clamp meter), you need **authorisation, a risk assessment, suitable PPE and a meter with the right CAT rating**. Permission from a passing staff member is not authorisation. Dead tests are done on isolated circuits, by a competent person, using safe isolation.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: If you find a real danger during the evaluation, such as **exposed live busbars in a board in a school corridor**, have it made safe and tell the client at once, in writing. Do not wait for the final report. A board blocked by pallets is also a safety issue, because it must be reachable in an emergency.

sections.title: Gathering evidence: inspection, sampling and interviews

blocks.p: Look at boards, wiring, accessories, earthing and bonding, equipment and the standby systems. Check that **each board's circuit chart matches the circuits it feeds**: if it does not, people will isolate the wrong circuit. Note damage, heat marks, rust, poor joints, missing covers, blocked access, and anything that departs from the specification.

In a large building you cannot inspect everything. A useful **sample** takes items from **each floor, area and type**, not just the rooms nearest the lift, the newest rooms or those the manager suggests. If faults are found, **widen the sample**: in a 200-room hotel, a 20-room check that finds problems leads to more rooms, and to the cause.

Maintenance staff know about trips, faults, changes and workarounds that are not on record. Ask what trips, when, what has been added, and what has been repaired. Do not ask them to carry out the evaluation, and do not use the talk to find someone to blame.

Every finding is recorded **at the time**, with its exact **location** (board, circuit, room), a **dated photo**, and the **reading or measurement**. Memory, guesses based on the age of a building, and what a tenant says by telephone are not evidence. As team leader, insist that each finding is recorded with its location and evidence before the team moves on.

head: Finding
Weak record
Good record
rows: 'Main board, breaker 14, terminal L1, 68 °C at 42 A, photo 17, 10 March'
'Kitchen outlet circuit 7, no RCD, 30 mA required by the specification, photo 22'
'Board B, way 5 labelled lights, feeds the A/C, photo 9'

blocks.h: Compliance checks on a new installation

blocks.p: Build a **checklist from the specification**: materials, cable types and sizes, containment, devices, labels, earthing and bonding, and the tests required. Check the work against it. If the specification asked for armoured cable to a pump house but PVC cable in plastic conduit was fitted, record that it does not meet the specification and refer it to the client and the contractor: do not accept it because it works today, do not rip it out without telling anyone, and do not change the specification to match the work. Check that the test results are complete, signed, within limits and taken with calibrated instruments.

head: Result
Meaning
rows: Small items to finish by agreed dates.
Not accepted until defects are corrected
A non-conformance that must be put right and rechecked.

sections.title: Capacity, balance, logging and power quality

blocks.p: **Spare capacity (headroom)** is the difference between the supply's rating and its peak demand. Check the real peak with a **logger** rather than the nameplates alone.

head: Sum
Method
Example
rows: Existing peak + new load used at the same time
Compare new peak with the lowest rating in the chain
72 + 36 = 108 A on a 100 A main: no
Design 40 A, logged 58 A: loads have grown

blocks.p: Capacity is judged along the whole chain: the **service, main switch, main cable, board busbars, sub-main and breakers**. The weakest part limits the rest. A school adding a computer lab to an existing sub-board checks the **sub-main rating, its logged demand and its spare ways** first, not the make of the computers.

ul: A logger records voltage, current on each line and the neutral, power, power factor and harmonics over days or weeks.
It is left for **at least a week** so that it sees the real peaks and patterns over normal days, including the busiest.
It is connected by a competent person with authorisation, a risk assessment, PPE and a CAT-rated instrument.
The number of readings = readings per hour × hours: every 10 minutes for 7 days is 6 × 24 × 7 = 1 008 readings.

blocks.p: On a 110/220 V board with mostly resistive 110 V loads, the neutral carries the **difference** between the two line currents. If line 1 is 52 A and line 2 is 30 A, about 22 A flows in the neutral: the lines are out of balance. The recommendation is to move circuits from the heavier line to the lighter one.

head: Observation
What to do
rows: Voltage falls to 98 V at the far end of a 110 V circuit when a photocopier runs
Compare with the specification's limit; check volt drop (cable size, length) and joints.
Lights dim each time a large compressor starts (a **voltage sag**)
Measure the voltage at the board and the circuit during starting, with a logger; look at cable size, joints and the supply.
110 V circuit reads 101 V at full load

blocks.p: **Harmonics** are unwanted currents at whole multiples of the 50 Hz supply frequency, caused by electronic loads such as computers, LED drivers and drives. They make the neutral carry more current than expected, overheat transformers and trip some devices. Look for a neutral current larger than the line imbalance explains, then consider a larger neutral or filters.
A power bill that charges for low power factor points to motor loads. Measure the load, then consider **power factor correction** with capacitors. Reactive power is shown in **kVAR**.

A server room that trips twice a month after more servers were added to one RCD-protected circuit is probably suffering from the **normal earth leakage of each server adding up** on the one RCD. The cure is to spread the servers over more circuits, not to fit a larger RCD.
A thermal camera shows the surface temperatures of boards, joints and cables, so poor connections, overloaded parts and unbalanced loads appear as **hot spots** without switching anything off.

head: Rule
Why
rows: Survey when the building is on normal or heavy load, after some hours of running
Heat depends on the current: on a light load a bad joint may not show.
Record the **load current** at the time
So hot spots can be compared fairly, and judged against the load at peak.
Set the camera's **emissivity** for the surface
Shiny metal reflects heat and gives false readings.
Take a normal photo with each thermal image
Covers are removed only by an authorised person, with a risk assessment and PPE, or viewing windows are used
It is live work: it needs control.
Compare each part with a **similar part carrying a similar load** (the **delta T**)
Comparing like with like makes a real defect stand out.

blocks.p: Example: one breaker terminal at 68 °C while identical terminals carrying a similar current are at 41 °C: delta T = 27 °C. The most likely cause is a loose or poor connection. Reporting priority is usually set in **bands** from the client's or the specification's rules (a small difference is watched, a moderate one repaired at the next planned outage, a large one repaired urgently). After repair, **resurvey** to confirm.

ul: Compare today's test results with the past ones. **A steady fall** in insulation resistance, such as 200 MΩ, then 90 MΩ, then 15 MΩ at yearly tests, is a warning sign even when every reading is above the minimum: find the cause (moisture, heat, damage, age).

Rubber-insulated cable from the 1970s that cracks and crumbles when moved is at the end of its **service life**: recommend rewiring, starting at once where it is worst. Painting it, avoiding touching it, or raising breaker sizes does not make it safe.
Compare with the design: logged peaks well above the designed maximum demand suggest growth, so check cable and device ratings.
Check that the circuit chart matches the board.

blocks.p: An earth electrode that read 12 Ω when new and now reads 85 Ω against a design value of 20 Ω has deteriorated, probably by a corroded rod or joint. Recommend finding and fixing the cause: re-making the joint, replacing or adding electrodes, then re-testing. Do not accept it because it is 'still connected', do not remove the rod, and do not fit a larger breaker to make up for it.

A hotel whose transfer switch failed to change over to the generator twice last year does not have a working standby system, even though the generator starts. Find and fix the cause, then **prove it with a witnessed test**.
Safety comes first, before any evaluation.

flow: Make sure the supply is off and locked off at the main switch; confirm with JPS that its service is isolated if the service cable is damaged
Prove dead with a tester checked before and after
Make sure any generator cannot start, and that its changeover switch cannot back-feed
Treat any solar PV array as **live in daylight**: damaged panels and DC cables still make voltage
Walk the site and record the damage, including the height the water reached
Decide which equipment must be replaced
Test insulation and dry cables under competent supervision where they can be saved
Report what must be repaired, and in what order, before the supply is restored

head: Item
After flood water
rows: Outlets, boards, breakers and RCDs that were under water
Replace them, or have them checked as the maker says, before use. Looking dry, hair-drying or checking only above the waterline is not enough.
Dry and test the insulation; replace where it is suspect.
Usually replaced, or checked and approved by the maker's guidance.
A trained person makes the DC side safe; washing the panels does not make them safe.

blocks.note: After a hurricane, falling trees and flooded ground floors hide many dangers: live damaged service cables, water in boards, back-feeding generators and live PV. The evaluator treats everything as live until proved dead.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: An energy evaluation finds where a building uses energy, what could be saved, and whether the saving pays for the work.

flow: Collect a year of bills and note the energy used, maximum demand, power factor and charges
Take a **baseline**: the measurements taken before any change, so that savings can be compared later
List the main users and their hours of use
Identify improvements: LED lighting, controls, power factor correction, A/C settings, shifting loads
Work out the saving and the cost of each
Calculate the simple payback and consider other effects
After the work, measure again and compare with the baseline

head: Sum
Method
Example
rows: 1.5 kW × 2 h × 30 days = 90 kWh a month

blocks.p: **Worked example.** 120 old fittings of 70 W are replaced by LED fittings of 24 W, lit 10 hours a day for 260 days. Saving per fitting 46 W; for 120 = 5.52 kW. Hours 2 600 a year; energy saved 14 352 kWh. At J$60 per kWh that is J$861 120 a year. If the LED fittings cost J$1 800 000, the simple payback is 1 800 000 ÷ 861 120 = about 2.1 years.

Also consider: whether the new fittings give the **light levels** the rooms need; sensors and controls for more savings; longer life and less upkeep; the lower heat, which reduces the A/C load; how the old fittings will be disposed of safely. A **low load factor** means the supply is large for the energy used, so peak-shaving or load shifting may reduce demand charges.

blocks.note: **Corridors with old 58 W fluorescent fittings lit 24 hours a day** are a good LED target, but taking out every second fitting without a study, or switching corridors off at night, may be unsafe for guests. Always evaluate the options with savings and payback worked out.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Six months after an energy evaluation, the client asks whether the changes worked. Measure again, under similar conditions, and compare with the baseline. Asking staff, or pointing out that nobody has complained, is not evidence.

Score each defect for **likelihood** (how likely it is to cause harm) and **severity** (how bad the harm would be), each from 1 to 5. **Risk score = likelihood × severity**, up to 25. Order the recommendations by risk: **danger to people first**, then damage, then savings. Do not order them by cost, by floor or by the order you happened to find them.

head: Example defect
Likelihood
Severity
Score
Action
rows: Exposed live parts in a board staff open often
Make safe at once; report in writing the same day
Missing RCD on outlets beside a kitchen sink

head: Option
Good
Not so good
rows: Does not solve overload or age; faults keep coming
Fixes the main risks and adds capacity
Highest cost; building empty or worked in stages

blocks.p: Give the client options with **costs, benefits, risks and a recommendation**. One option only, or the most expensive 'to be safe', or no option, is not a basis for a decision. Compare options by **life-cycle cost**: buying, running, upkeep and replacing over time. A board that is cheaper to buy but has a short life and no spares can cost more overall.

Total = labour + materials (+ plant, testing, fees, contingency), then GCT at the current rate. Example: 40 hours at J$2 500 an hour = J$100 000; plus J$150 000 of materials = **J$250 000 before GCT**.

head: Part
Contents
rows: The overall finding and the most urgent recommendations, in a few lines, for a busy reader.
What was evaluated, what was not, and why.
How the work was done: inspection, sampling, logging, thermal survey and tests, with instruments and their calibration.
By area or system, each with exact location, evidence (photo, reading) and risk score.
Ranked, with timescales, rough costs, and options where there is a choice.
Logger graphs, test schedules, thermal images.

blocks.p: A recommendation says **what**, **where** and **by when**: 'Replace the 30-year-old kitchen sub-board within three months.' 'Improve the electrical system soon', 'Some of the boards are not very good' and 'Look at the wiring when there is some time' tell the client nothing. Each finding gives its exact location (board, circuit and room) so the repair team can find and fix the right item.

flow: Send the report ahead of the meeting
Go through it with the client, starting with any danger
Answer questions in plain words
Agree the next steps in writing
Follow up: check that repairs were done and resurvey where needed

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can list the reasons for evaluating an installation, and the ones that are not reasons.
I can agree a purpose and scope in writing, and say what to evaluate against.
I can plan the team, instruments, risk assessment and permits.
I can handle missing drawings and records.
I can take a fair sample and widen it when faults are found.
I can record each finding with location, photo and reading.
I can evaluate a new installation against its specification and give an accept or reject decision.
I can work out spare capacity and whether a new load fits.
I can plan and use a power logger safely and read line balance, sags, harmonics and power factor.
I can run and rank a thermal survey, with emissivity, load current and delta T.
I can spot ageing from trends in insulation resistance and a deteriorating earth electrode.
I can evaluate an installation safely after a flood or hurricane.
I can take a baseline and work out kWh, load factor, savings and simple payback.
I can score and rank risks by likelihood × severity.
I can compare repair, upgrade and replacement, with life-cycle cost.
I can write a report with a summary, ranked findings and costed options, and present it danger first.
I can show that improvements worked by measuring again.

terms: Measurements taken before any change, so savings can be compared later.
The temperature difference between similar parts under similar load.
How well a surface gives off heat; set on a thermal camera for accurate readings.
Unwanted currents at whole multiples of 50 Hz, caused by electronic loads.
The cost of buying, running, maintaining and replacing something over its life.
The highest average demand in kW over a set short period.
An instrument left at a board to record voltage, current and power over time.
A short fall in supply voltage, for example when a large motor starts.
A selection of items, taken fairly, that stands for the whole.
The number of years an item is expected to last in use.
The cost of an improvement ÷ its yearly saving.
The difference between a supply's rating and its peak demand.

c1.title: A new computer lab at a Lucea school
c1.text: A high school in Lucea, Hanover, wants to add a computer lab to an existing block. The block's sub-main and main switch are rated 160 A. A week-long log on the main board shows a peak of 118 A. On the 110 V circuits, line 1 peaks at 66 A and line 2 at 48 A. The new lab will add about 30 A that runs at the same time as the existing peak, and the school hopes to add a 25 A science room later.

c2.title: A thermal survey at a Montego Bay printery
c2.text: A printery in Montego Bay asks for a thermal survey of its main board during a normal working day. The camera shows one breaker terminal at 80 °C. Three identical terminals carrying similar current are at 46 °C. The load was about 30% of normal when the images were taken. The main busbars are bright, polished copper, and the camera is on its default emissivity setting. Insulation tests on the main sub-main over three years read 150, 60 and 12 megohms.

c3.title: An energy evaluation for a Portmore call centre
c3.text: A call centre in Portmore, St Catherine, has 80 old fittings of 58 W, lit 12 hours a day for 300 days a year. LED replacements of 20 W would cost J$1 200 000 in all. The tariff is J$55 per kWh. The bills show 16 200 kWh used in a 30-day month and a maximum demand of 36 kW. The manager wants to be sure the savings are real after the work.

c4.title: After the flood at a Bluefields primary school
c4.text: A primary school in Bluefields, Westmoreland, was flooded to 400 mm in the ground-floor classrooms during a hurricane. The school has a diesel generator with an automatic transfer switch, a roof-mounted PV array with several broken panels, outlets and a sub-board low on a classroom wall, and a damaged service drop. The principal wants the lights back on before the term begins and asks the evaluator to start at once.

c5.title: Accepting a new plaza at Morant Bay
c5.text: A contractor says a new plaza in Morant Bay is complete and asks the client to accept it. The specification calls for armoured cable on the underground feeder, but PVC cable in plastic conduit was fitted. The contractor's test records are unsigned for two boards. The evaluator finds exposed live terminals in an open meter room that shoppers can enter, and a missing label on one sub-board. The client needs the report before deciding whether to pay the final instalment.

questions.q: What percentage of the 160 A rating does the logged peak of 118 A use?
o: About 36%
About 136%
About 74%
About 26%
questions.why: 118 ÷ 160 × 100 = 73.75%, about 74%. Always divide by the rating and say what the percentage is of; the remaining 26% or so is the headroom.

questions.q: With the new lab's 30 A at the same time, what is the new peak, and does it fit the 160 A rating?
o: 148 A, which fits but leaves little headroom
88 A, which leaves a lot of spare capacity
148 A, which is over the rating of 160 A
30 A, since only the new load matters
questions.why: 118 + 30 = 148 A, under 160 A, so the lab fits, with only 12 A to spare. The evaluator should say so plainly and warn the school about further growth.

questions.q: If the 25 A science room is added later at the same time, what should the evaluator recommend?
o: Nothing, since 173 A is close enough to 160 A
Fit a larger breaker on the existing sub-main cable
Move the science room onto line 2 and carry on
Plan an upgrade: 173 A is over the 160 A rating
questions.why: 148 + 25 = 173 A is more than the 160 A rating. Options are an upgrade of the service, main switch, cable and board, or load management, with costs. A larger breaker on the old cable would remove its protection.

questions.q: Line 1 peaks at 66 A and line 2 at 48 A on the 110 V circuits. What does this show, with resistive loads?
o: The board is well balanced, so no action is needed
About 18 A flows in the neutral, so the lines are out of balance
About 114 A flows in the neutral, from the two lines together
The meter is faulty, since the lines should be exactly equal
questions.why: The neutral carries the difference, 66 − 48 = 18 A. The recommendation is to move some 110 V circuits from line 1 to line 2, which lowers the neutral current and the volt drop.

questions.q: The hot terminal is at 80 °C and identical terminals are at 46 °C. What is the delta T, and what is the most likely cause?
o: 126 °C; the breaker is overloaded by design
34 °C; the room is too cool for the breaker
46 °C; the camera is set to the wrong palette
34 °C; a loose or poor connection at that terminal
questions.why: Delta T is the difference between like parts on similar load: 80 − 46 = 34 °C. A single terminal much hotter than its identical neighbours points to a loose or poor connection.

questions.q: The images were taken at about 30% of normal load. What should the evaluator conclude?
o: The fault is minor, because the load was light
It may be worse at full load, so repeat on a heavier load
The survey is finished, since the camera has found it
The temperature rise will fall when the load rises
questions.why: Heat depends on current, roughly with its square, so at 30% load a bad joint is much cooler than at full load. Survey on normal or heavy load, and record the load current with each image.

questions.q: The bright, polished copper busbars read cooler than they really are. What setting must the evaluator check?
o: The camera's emissivity setting for that surface
The camera's battery level and brightness
The colour palette used for the image
The distance of the camera from the floor
questions.why: Shiny metal gives off heat poorly and reflects its surroundings, so the camera under-reads unless emissivity is set correctly, or the surface is treated. A normal photo is taken with each image to show the location.

questions.q: The sub-main's insulation readings are 150, 60 and 12 megohms over three years. What should the evaluator say, if all are above the minimum?
o: All three pass, so nothing needs to be done
The test instrument is faulty, since readings should stay equal
The steady fall is a warning: find the cause and act
The cable is improving, because the readings are lower
questions.why: Each reading passes, but the trend is steeply downward, which suggests moisture, heat or ageing. The evaluator reports the trend, finds the cause and recommends action before the cable fails.

questions.q: What is the yearly energy saving from changing the 80 fittings from 58 W to 20 W?
o: 3 040 kWh
7 200 kWh
questions.why: Each fitting saves 38 W; 80 × 38 = 3 040 W = 3.04 kW. Hours = 12 × 300 = 3 600 a year; 3.04 × 3 600 = 10 944 kWh.

questions.q: At J$55 per kWh, what is the call centre's yearly money saving, and so its simple payback?
o: J$601 920 a year; payback about 0.5 years
J$10 944 a year; payback about 110 years
J$65 340 a year; payback about 18 years
J$601 920 a year; payback about 2.0 years
questions.why: Saving = 10 944 × 55 = J$601 920. Payback = cost ÷ yearly saving = 1 200 000 ÷ 601 920 = about 2.0 years, not 0.5 (that divides the wrong way round).

questions.q: From the bills, what is the call centre's load factor?
questions.why: Average demand = 16 200 kWh ÷ (30 × 24 h) = 22.5 kW. Load factor = 22.5 ÷ 36 = 0.625, or 62.5%.

questions.q: How can the evaluator show the manager that the savings are real?
o: Point out that the staff have not complained about it
Send the first report again with a new date on it
Take a baseline, then measure again and compare
Ask the staff if the offices seem brighter than before
questions.why: A baseline is the set of measurements taken before the change. Measuring again under similar conditions and comparing is the only way to show the real saving.

questions.q: What should the evaluator do first at the flooded school?
o: Switch the supply back on to see what still works
Walk through the classrooms with a thermal camera
Dry the outlets and the board with a hair dryer
Isolate, lock off, prove dead, stop the generator
questions.why: Safety comes first. Isolate and prove dead, confirm with JPS that the damaged service is isolated, and stop the generator and its transfer switch from back-feeding.

questions.q: What must the evaluator say about the broken PV panels?
o: They are safe to approach, since they are broken
They still make voltage in daylight: a shock risk
They will work again as soon as they are washed
They can be reset from the inverter's screen
questions.why: A PV module produces voltage whenever light falls on it, even if broken, and its DC cables stay live. They are treated as live until a trained person has made them safe.

questions.q: The sub-board and outlets that stood in 400 mm of water look dry. What should the report say?
o: They may be used again once they look dry inside
Only the outlets above the waterline need checking
Replace them, or have them checked as the maker says
They can be used if a GFCI is added in front of them
questions.why: Flood water leaves silt and moisture inside equipment, so equipment that has been under water is replaced, or checked and approved by the maker's guidance, before it is energised.

questions.q: How should the report order its recommendations before the supply is restored?
o: By risk: make safe first, then repairs, then upgrades
Cheapest repairs first, to get the lights back quickly
Top floor first, then the ground floor after that
In the order the evaluator happened to find them
questions.why: Danger to people comes first, such as the damaged service, the PV and flooded equipment. Then damage repairs, then improvements. The principal's wish to reopen does not change the order of risk.

questions.q: The feeder is PVC cable in plastic conduit, not armoured as specified. What should the evaluator do?
o: Accept it, since it works today
Record it as not meeting the specification and refer it
Have it dug up at once without telling the contractor
Change the specification to match the work done
questions.why: A departure from the specification goes on the non-conformance list with its location and evidence. The client and contractor then decide what to do; the evaluator does not accept it, change the specification or act alone.

questions.q: Exposed live terminals are found in a meter room that shoppers can enter. How should this be handled?
o: Note it for the final report due next week
Photograph it and continue with the evaluation
Tell the shoppers to keep out of the meter room
Have it made safe at once and tell the client
questions.why: A danger to people is dealt with immediately and reported in writing, before the final report. It is also shown first in the report and the presentation.

questions.q: Which finding scores highest on likelihood (1 to 5) × severity (1 to 5)?
o: Missing label on a sub-board: likelihood 3, severity 2
Unsigned test records: likelihood 5, severity 1
Exposed live terminals: likelihood 4, severity 5
PVC conduit instead of armoured cable: likelihood 2, severity 3
questions.why: 4 × 5 = 20 against 6, 5 and 6 for the others. The score directs the client's money and time to the greatest risk.

questions.q: How should the evaluator present the plaza report to the client?
o: Send it ahead, go through it danger first, agree next steps
Leave it with the receptionist and wait for a reply
Start with the cheapest items and end with the dangers
Cover the good news first, so that the client stays calm
questions.why: A report is presented in a meeting, in plain words, starting with any danger, and the next steps are agreed and written down. Putting the danger at the end risks the client never acting on it.
